groundTruthNarrative: Agency spend tripled mainly because Larchmere bought 2.6 times as many agency hours; the contractual wage-index escalator explains only about a quarter of the increase. Volume is driven by a reinforcing loop. Policy NUR-114 bars agency RNs from charge and precepting and requires buddy orientation, so every rise in agency share concentrates those duties on a shrinking group of charge-qualified permanent RNs. Exhaustion rises, and about two quarters later they resign, creating more vacancies and more agency use. The 4 West pilot cut the load without changing pay or agency share; resignations fell from four a quarter to one, but only after the delay, which is why the CNO judged it a failure at the end of Q1 2026. Regional wage inflation and St. Brennan's opening are real external pressures that amplify the loop, but resignations began rising in Q3 2024, well before St. Brennan's recruited. The 2025 bonus did not reduce vacancies and added preceptor load. The proposed bonus, funded by cutting the charge and preceptor differentials, would feed the loop. Agency use and falls co-occur, but acuity confounds the comparison.

answers.rationale: The CNO frames the spend as a rate problem, but the finance decomposition (E2) shows billed hours rose from 63,200 to 162,900 (2.6x) while the average rate rose 18%; volume accounts for about 77% of the $12.7M increase and rate for about 23%. Price is a real but minority component, so 'mainly a price effect' is contradicted.

Every link is evidenced: vacancies rise with agency hours (E2, E3); policy concentrates charge, precepting and orientation on permanent RNs (E4); load per charge-qualified RN more than doubled and tracks unit agency share (E5); lagged load predicts resignations and resignations predict later agency share (E6); exit interviews and the survey name this burden (E8, E14). The 4 West pilot (E7) reduced load and, after a delay, resignations, while agency share, pay and manager stayed constant and matched units did not change. No rival explains the unit-level variation under a uniform pay scale.

Resignations rose from 18 in Q2 2024 to 24 in Q3 2024 and reached 41 in Q4 2025 (E3). St. Brennan's did not advertise RN posts until October 2025 and opened in March 2026 (E11), so it cannot have started the rise. It is a real destination for some leavers (19 of 98 known destinations in 2026, E9) and an amplifier, but the claim that it started the rise is contradicted by timing.

The pay gap is real and widening (E10) and pay is a stated reason for a minority of leavers (17%, E8; 74 survey comments versus 212 on orientation, E14), so pay is contributing. But all units share one pay scale while resignation rates vary with charge and orientation load (E5, E6), and 4 West cut resignations from 4 to 1 per quarter with no pay change while matched units on the same pay did not improve (E7). Pay cannot be the primary driver.

The only evidence is two conflicting accounts: Talent Acquisition says 41 days is in line with peers, and a nurse manager says candidates are lost to faster offers (E17). The applicant tracking system records no withdrawals by stage or reason and no competitor comparison exists. Flat hire counts (E3) are consistent with either view. The claim is live but neither established nor refuted.

The mechanism is a written rule: agency RNs may not take charge or precept and each needs two buddy-orientation shifts from a permanent RN (E4). The load moved with agency share across units (5.8 vs 2.4 shifts per month) and over time, and on every high-agency unit the rise in load followed the rise in agency share (E5). Mechanism, temporal order and covariation together establish causation; the 4 West pilot shows the link can be cut only by deliberately reassigning those duties (E7).

E6 alone is correlational, with the analyst's own caveat. The 4 West pilot (E7) is an intervention with comparison units chosen in advance: load fell, exhaustion fell, and resignations fell from 4 to 2 to 1 two quarters later, while agency share, pay and manager were unchanged and 5 West and 6 East stayed flat or rose. The two-quarter lag matches the lag peak in E6 and the note that early leavers had already committed to leave. The CNO's 'it did not work' (E1) reads the result before the delay had elapsed.

High-agency units do have higher fall rates (0.71 vs 0.38), so the two co-occur. But those units also have higher acuity and older patients, no adjusted unit-month analysis exists, and falls are not linked to the assigned nurse (E16). Confounding by acuity and age remains live, so causation is not established and the edge is not unknown either.

The 2025 bonus raised hires (64 vs 52) but the vacancy rate kept rising, from 8.6% to 10.9% during the bonus and 12.6% six months later; 24 of 64 bonus hires had left by month 15, mostly right after the clawback ended, and preceptor shifts rose 31% (E13). The evidence counts against a sustained reduction in vacancies.

The Vantage contract escalator adjusts bill rates each January by the change in the state RN wage index, and billed base rates moved by exactly the index changes of 9.4% and 7.9% (E2, E10). A contractual mechanism with exact covariation establishes the link.

The bonus is funded by removing the charge and preceptor differentials (E12), the only pay that recognizes the group already overloaded and leaving (E8, E14). Charge-qualified nurses say they will drop the qualification or leave (E15). Each bonus hire also needs a 12-week preceptorship (E12), adding load to that same group, and the 2025 bonus did not reduce vacancies (E13). The action feeds the established causal loop (E7) and is likely to worsen it.

This acts directly on the established causal link (charge and orientation load to resignations) on the units where that load is highest (E5), using an intervention that cut resignations against matched controls (E7). Monitoring at two and three quarters respects the observed delay. It is the best supported substantive action.

A three-year outsourcing commitment would be justified only if slow time-to-hire were a material constraint (H5), which the evidence leaves unknown (E17). The applicant funnel data (Q1) could settle it. Committing now is not justified, but nothing shows it would do harm.

The falls rationale rests on an association confounded by acuity (E16). The remedy, mandatory overtime for permanent staff on two step-down units, adds load to the group whose load causally drives resignations (E5, E7) and who already report unsafe charge and precepting frequency (E14). It acts on an unestablished cause and intensifies the established driver of the loop, so it is likely to worsen outcomes.

The escalator causally passes regional wage inflation into bill rates, and framework vendors quote 6-8% lower for the same credentialing (E2), so renegotiating at renewal is sensible and low-risk. But the action makes rate renegotiation the primary lever for cutting agency spend, while rate accounts for only about 23% of the increase and volume, driven by the resignation loop, for about 77% (E2). As a primary strategy it is misdirected, so it is reasonable but not among the best actions.

The core loop is established by a written mechanism, covariation, lag analysis and a controlled pilot (E4-E7), which is enough to commit to A2 and to reject A1 and A4. The open questions (time-to-hire, agency and falls) bear on secondary actions, not on the main intervention.
